articleTitle: Optical computing: A field in flux
abstract: War has broken out. A thousand missiles thunder off their launch pads halfway around the world, from a country hell-bent on destroying the United States. Only 25 minutes - 1500 precious seconds - remain to destroy them before they reenter the atmosphere over their targets. By then the number will have multiplied into as many as 10 000 warheads, many of them live nuclear heads, some decoys. How can they all be individually tracked and the live warheads annihilated in space before they hit their targets?

articleTitle: Communicating in the technical office: The Technical and Office Protocols specification, released in November, will be tempered in the fires of realistic applications
abstract: The lack of international standard communication protocols for computers and other programmable equipment leaves buyers between the proverbial rock and hard place. They can buy proprietary systems from a single supplier and get instantaneous communications compatibility, but they will almost certainly face interconnection problems later if they add equipment from other suppliers. Or they can buy from several suppliers initially to get the systems that perform the best and cost the least, but they will have to purchase expensive custom interfaces to connect the different systems.

articleTitle: The quest for ballistic action: Avoiding collisions during electron transport to increase switching speeds is the goal of the ultimate transistor
abstract: Semiconductor devices that operate faster than those made with current silicon technology are the goal of laboratories around the world. The purpose is to speed up computers that are already capable of high data rates. One “ultimate” being sought is the world's fastest transistor: one that takes advantage of ballistic transport of electrons.

articleTitle: Gyroscopes may cease spinning: Optical gyroscopes without moving parts are more reliable and more rugged than conventional mechanical systems
abstract: After 20 years of development, the first commercial optical gyroscope - the ring laser gyro - is flying regularly in civilian aircraft and has logged 2.5 million flight hours to date. Ring laser gyros, or RLGs, have replaced mechanical gyros as standard equipment in Boeing 757 and 767 jetliners and the Airbus 310, and are being eyed for a variety of next-generation military systems. The optical gyro's greater reliability, wide dynamic range, and ability to with-stand high-g fields and harsh environments make it superior to mechanical gyroscopes, with their spinning rotors and complex gimballed mounts.

articleTitle: The compact disk ROM: How it works: An offshoot of the compact digital audio disk, this multimegabyte storage technique is revolutionizing database technology
abstract: In the world of the CD-ROM, paper is largely obsolete. So are file clerks for retrieving information. A filing cabinet's worth of records can be stored on one disk, as can a 20-volume, 9-million-word encyclopedia or financial data on 10000 corporations. Even more remarkable, any piece of information in each mass of data can be made available on demand in seconds.

Almost every frequent flier has a tale of supposed horror, includingmassive thunderstorms, direct hits by lightning, and abortive landings and takeoffs. In such moments the traveler may wonder briefly just how safe flying is, but such concerns are put aside when the next reservation is made.

articleTitle: Fiber-optic gyroscopes: In harsh, confining environments this advanced gyroscope, a close cousin to the ring laser gyro, offers great advantages
abstract: Fiber-optic gyroscopes are the stuff of an applications engineer's dreams. They can be small and extremely rugged. They turn on instantly, have long shelf life, are virtually maintenance-free, and will be low in cost. As “strapdown” devices, they do not require expensive gimbaled mounting systems, and they are free of the low-rotation-rate lock-in that causes other optical gyro types to produce false zero outputs.

articleTitle: Minis and mainframes: Microcomputers as we know them may disappear as sophisticated microprocessors reach toward mainframe capability; more powerful supercomputers are introduced
abstract: Fifty years from now, historians of computer science may regard the VAX 11/780 as the last true minicomputer. Spiraling capabilities of single-chip VLSI procesors and declining memory costs are combining to blur the distinctions between the high end of microprocessor-based computers and the multiboard minis of the past.

articleTitle: Communications: Coherent optical communication shows promise, the FCC continues on its path of deregulation, and satellite communications go high-frequency
abstract: Few fields of electronics are as firmly entrenched as communications, yet revolutionary progress continues to unwind year after year, each development as exciting in its own way as Marconi's experiments with wireless telegraphy. Last year giant steps were taken in bringing the integrated services digital network (ISDN) to fruition around the world. This progress was aided by the continued installation of fiber-optic systems.

articleTitle: The promise of the Kalina cycle: Using an ammonia-water mixture, the Kalina steam cycle may permit thermal-mechanical-electrical energy conversion efficiencies of 45 percent
abstract: New technologies come and go, but the Rankine steam cycle goes on forever - or so it seemed until Alexander I. Kalina found a better way. Power engineers have known for years that heat can be generated more efficiently in a boiler if a mixture like ammonia and water is used as the working fluid, but no one had figured out how to condense the working fluid mixture at normal heat rejection temperatures. Kalina, a former top Soviet energy official who emigrated to the United States and now lives in Houston, I Texas, solved the problem, at least in theory. Now it must be determined whether his theory holds up in practice.

articleTitle: Microprocessors: New architectures increase speed, and RISC processors are moving from university laboratories into commercial products
abstract: The 32-bit microprocessor is no longer “emerging” by 1985 it had become the technology of choice for virtually any advanced application. Four years after announcement of the first commercial 32-bit processor, three general families of 32-bit design can be discerned.

articleTitle: A surge for solid state: Revitalization of the U.S. semiconductor industry may depend on supplying unconnected transistors and letting the buyer specify on-chip interconnections
abstract: The loss of leadership in the 256K RAM market to Japan is merely a symptom of the revolutionary upheaval in the U.S. semiconductor industry. Can the industry be rejuvenated? Ironically its greatest hope lies in a return to its roots: supplying unconnected transistors on integrated circuits so that users and algorithm designers can specify the on-chip connections according to the needs of the applications.

Many advances in materials technology have contributed to the speed of present silicon transistors. Over the years these advances have led to dramatic reductions in the two critical dimensions that determine the speed of a bipolar transistor: the width of the stripe-shaped emitter and the thickness of the base.

Debate over whether to deregulate the electric utility industry has widened in recent months. Deregulation is one possible outcome of a number of competitive moves in the industry, as discussed in the preceding article.

The most convincing evidenceto date ofthe existenceof true ballistic electron transport in semiconductorswas demonstrated experimentallylast year. With a technique known as electron energy spectroscopy, researchers probed the energy distribution of electrons traveling through a device.

articleTitle: 'Gold-plated' design: Redundancy and extremely high safety factors allow aircraft to withstand forces far exceeding those encountered during routine flights
abstract: Unlike the Concorde, the Boeing 727 was not designed to travel at the speed of sound or faster. But in the air over Saginaw, Mich., in April 1979, that is exactly what one did. A Boeing 727, spiraling in an uncontrollable dive from 39 000 feet, reached a calculated Mach number of 0.96 - enough to put parts of the craft into transsonic territory, based on the varying airspeeds around the fuselage.

articleTitle: Robots for fun and profit: A new breed of experimenter is more artist than scientist, yet this work sometimes pays off handsomely
abstract: It is an unlikely electronics laboratory that Gene Oldfield runs in downtown Sacramento, Calif. In one corner is an unmade bed. A lanky dog - a sorrel saluki named Algebra - is curled up under a bench, and flanks of toy robots are perched on the windowsills. Abstract paintings and collages adorn the walls, and an espresso maker and board games share shelf space with power transistors, electric motors, single-board computers, and oscilloscopes.

articleTitle: New times at the faa: Since deregulation, the number of pilots, planes, and airlines has overwhelmed the Federal Aviation Administration
abstract: Whenever there is a fatal air accident in the United States, critics inevitably charge that the Federal Aviation Administration cannot keep the skies safe. And since Aug. 31, when a small Piper PA-28 private plane collided with an Aeromexico DC-9 jetliner near Los Angeles, the U.S. Congress and air safety advocates have again focused their attention on the FAA.

articleTitle: Detroit's 1987 models: New electronic inroads: Suspensions are the latest conquest in the trend toward total electronic control of all major automotive subsystems
abstract: Few, if any, major mechanical parts of a car cannot be controlled electronically today. Electronically controlled ignitions, engines, displays, on-board diagnostics - to name just a few subsystems - have all become commonplace. But who would have envisioned, just a few years ago, a production automobile with a control system that adjusts the car's ride automatically from soft to firm depending upon driving and road conditions at any instant? The 1987 turbo-powered Ford Thunderbird has it.

Throughout the summer of 1985 an internal debate raged within the Reagan administration: Should the United States continue to adhere to the unratified SALT II treaty - an agreement that many people believe the Soviet Union has violated? At issue was the fate of two U.S. ballistic-missile submarines: a new Ohio-class vessel, the Alaska, capable of launching Trident missiles, and an older Poseidon-missile submarine, the USS Sam Rayburn.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: A NASA design defect
abstract: The principal suspects in the Jan. 28 shuttle accident, as we write, are the gaskets, or O-rings, intended as the ultimate seal between segments of the solid rocket motors. Their potentiality for failure had been well known; their deterioration during previous missions had been well documented; and numerous alternate designs had been proposed.

articleTitle: U.S. semiconductor industry getting it together: Despite their history of intense competition, U.S. manufacturers are cooperating in research to gain an edge in the international marketplace
abstract: A little less than four years after the U.S. semiconductor industry set up a research consortium to help regain its technical edge in the face of growing Japanese dominance in the integrated circuit market, a few early results are beginning to reach the computer screens and development labs of the consortium's industrial sponsors, including IBM, Digital Equipment Corp., Du Pont, Hewlett-Packard, and AT&T. But the big question is: By the time major research fallout is expected, in the 1990s, will there be enough of the US. semiconductor industry left to take advantage of it?

articleTitle: How the promising PCC car was prematurely derailed: The U.S. electric streetcar industry failed to reap the rewards of its 1930s research, aimed at producing a revolutionary trolley car
abstract: Oct. 1, 1936, dawned cool and damp in New York City, another unmemorable day in the Great Depression, except for one event that at first glance appeared to be routine. Mayor Fiorello H. La Guardia snipped a blue ribbon strung across a section of trolley tracks at the Manhattan end of the Brooklyn Bridge to mark the start of service by a new generation of streetcars - the PCC car.

articleTitle: What price safety? Air travelers may be unaware that unless the U.S. Congress acts, increasing the margins of safety may be unaffordable as airlines compete for market share
abstract: Eight years of deregulation have witnessed airfares as low as $99 for travel from New York City to San Francisco, But would travelers be willing to pay more to, say, double the margin of safety for that 6-hour flight? Perhaps $100 more? Or $200?

articleTitle: Solid state: Economics and politics dominate the industry; nonetheless, application-specific and power-logic circuits spark new trends
abstract: Asked to sum up trends in the U.S. semiconductor industry last year, one expert said simply: “Business was lousy.” The industry was set back by markedly slowed sales that paralleled the slump in the computer industry.

While evolving lithographic and crystal growth technology gradually are allowing the construction of shorter transistors, the effort to reach the ultimate electron velocity - the ballistic limit - has the potential for dramatically increased frequency response. One particularly promising method for boosting the average electron velocity is to give the electrons a running start: introduce them into the active region as a directed beam at high velocity by a ballistic injector.

articleTitle: Photons in the service of electrons
abstract: “Electronics can make a 10-picosecond transistor, but it's very difficult to make a 10-picosecond wire,” remarked AT&T's Alan Huang. Not surprisingly, all investigators want to capitalize on the superiority of photons to electronics in handling communications and interconnections.

articleTitle: Industrial electronics: Computer-based manufacturing systems, expert systems, and process controllers continue to draw attention, as does robotry for the assembly of surface-mounted components
abstract: Innovations in industrial electronics in 1985 ranged from the availability of distributed controls for assembly lines to the application of artificial intelligence in self-tuning controllers.

A cursory look at consumer electronics products introduced in 1985 might lead to the conclusion that innovation had stopped. Few years in the recent past lacked an attempt by manufacturers to open up at least one new product category - 8-millimeter videocassettes, compact disk audio, stereo television broadcasting, laser disk video - attempts that were more or less successful. But last year manufacturers introduced nothing radically “new.”

articleTitle: The specialties: Experts identify the most outstanding developments or the most difficult problems in their fields
abstract: We asked experts in fields more specialized than those covered elsewhere in this report to identify the most pressing issues or the most telling breakthroughs in their own specialties. A number of responses were received, many of them from Presidents of IEEE Societies.

The authors survey the factors that have determined the success or failure of various PCs. The importance that consumers have attached to standard architectures is noted. However, it is pointed out that when hardware standards become established, manufacturers must push harder to differentiate their products from `clones'. It is argued that revolutionary advances in PC technology are not prompted by the users at whom the machines are targeted, but they are created by engineers, research and development teams. The advantages and disadvantages of open architecture are compared with those of closed architectures.

articleTitle: Special report/verification: Peacekeeping by technical means
abstract: Each day U.S. reconnaissance satellites and planes produce hundreds of images of the Soviet Union that must be interpreted. It is an imprecise and complicated process. Is that white blur near the building different from the blur in the last picture? Does that cluster of missile launchers near Plesetsk put the Soviets over the agreed limit?

articleTitle: Spectral lines: In the line of duty
abstract: Many of us did not know Judith Resnik or Gregory Jarvis personally. Yet there is pride for us in hearing the words “Judith Resnik, electrical engineer...” and “Gregory Jarvis, electrical engineer...”

The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers is unique. All other electrical engineering professional societies are nationalistic. The only other organization that could lay claim to the internationalism of the IEEE was one of its predecessors, the Institute of Radio Engineers.

articleTitle: Lessons learned: Challenges abound as designers tackle integrated software, artificial intelligence, and user-friendliness
abstract: During the spring of 1975 two men spent a month writing software at Harvard University. The focus of their work was a small metal box, slightly larger than a stereo receiver, called the MITS Altair.

articleTitle: Subzero engineering: At ¿40°F, with the wind howling at 60 miles per hour over permanently frozen ground, unconventional engineering techniques were required
abstract: The whine of the jet engines dropped in pitch as the pilot of the Alaska Airlines 727 throttled back and began the descent into Nome. Although it was but late afternoon, the November sky over Alaska was black, the stars obscured by a cloud cover. It was 1970 and I was a young electrical engineer aboard the plane in search of adventure, after two years as a computer designer and a year and a half as a U.S. Army commander in Korea.

articleTitle: Hero or scapegoat? Most standard practices of commercial airline pilots are safe, yet pilots are often blamed for accidents
abstract: Depending on whom you talk to, airline pilots either cause most plane accidents, or they're the only dependable cog in the air system, often pulling planes from certain disaster at the last second.

Last year 408 people were killed by terrorists in planes, airports, and airline ticket offices around the world, according to a report issued last February by U.S. Vice President George Bush's Task Force on Combatting Terrorism. A total of 329 were killed when a bomb exploded in the baggage compartment of an Air India Boeing 747 approaching Ireland on June 23. “The biggest single problem (in counterterrorism] is detecting bombs placed in baggage,” said Robert Kupperman, a senior advisor at Georgetown University's center for Strategic and International Studies In Washington, D.C., and the author of several books on combating terrorism. Despite a flurry of technological initiatives, dogs are still the most reliable bomb detectors, Kupperman said, although they are far from perfect. Expensive to train, dogs can also be foiled by masking odors or by well-sealed packages.

A few years back we wrote about individuals' 6370957circles of concern,” suggesting that each human being is surrounded by an invisible boundary that defines his or her interests. The circles may be small or large.

articleTitle: Software: The Strategic Defense Initiative brings into focus issues of software design, software development productivity, and complexity
abstract: A sociologist looking at software developments in 1985 might say it was a year for the democratizing of software. For years, complex tools like program analyzers and text editors specialized for a particular computer language have been available to artificial-intelligence researchers and other elite specialists. Last year such tools started to become available to the average software developer in industry. So-called programming environments address issues of program design and specification as well as the more familiar problems of writing program code. Last year also saw the introduction of some significant artificial-intelligence applications - not just the tools for building them.

How often have you been exposed to conversations that suggest employees are unhappy with or displeased about their bosses? If you're a city dweller, you need only listen to exchanges between strangers as they commute to work on public transportation. Another good place to overhear complaints is the elevator. In urban areas, the car pool is an ideal spot to learn about the shortcomings of managers.

articleTitle: The shrinking U.S. electric equipment market: What is eating away at U.S. manufacturers' share of the world market? An alleged European-Japanese cartel may be compounding the slowdown in U.S. growth
abstract: The U.S. heavy electric-power equipment industry is following the trail of the U.S. steel, clothing, and semiconductor industries: it is disappearing overseas.

articleTitle: Instrumentation: Powerful microprocessors and standard buses help advance modular card instrumentation; meanwhile bench test equipment gets new features
abstract: The trend toward digital processing in test instrumentation continues unabated. Advances in the performance of microprocessors and the linkage of personal computers and workstations to instrumentation last year increased not only data acquisition capability, but also the processing and analysis power of the instruments themselves.

articleTitle: Power and energy: Computers bring dramatic improvements in power management, permitting an increase in the wheeling of power and spurring the development of HVDC systems
abstract: The power utility industry in the United States, which has long operated as a controlled monopoly, appears headed for modification. Last year power companies found themselves, somewhat like the telephone utilities several years earlier, caught up in the market force that drives all private enterprise in the country: competition.

articleTitle: Medical electronics: Implantable defibrillators, cochlear devices, and lithotripters lead the list of recent developments
abstract: The man from Vancouver didn't feel well. Walking down the street, he suddenly felt faint. As he sat down on the sidewalk curb, he felt a sudden jolt pass through his body, as if someone had kicked him in the chest. After the jolt, he felt better. He stood up, hailed a cab, and went home.

'A five-year-old child can recognize faces, but a super Cray can't even recognize a handwritten character,' remarked Demetri Psaltis, associate professor of electrical engineering at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena. Yet a human being is lousy at algebra compared with a computer. What is it about a digital electronic computer that makes it so awkward for certain tasks versus the natural neural network of the brain?'

articleTitle: Transportation: AC propuision and the use of microprocessors for locomotive control and diagnostics may help an ailing railroad industry retrack itself
abstract: As railroads strive to cut operating and maintenance costs in an increasingly competitive transportation industry, AC propulsion and microprocessors figure prominently in their plans. New generations of locomotives and cars incorporating AC propulsion and microprocessors entered service last year, and the trend is destined to continue.

articleTitle: Lessons learned: Classic debates aired first by mainframe developers, then by minicomputer makers are discovered anew by the PC industry
abstract: After a decade of designing and building personal computers, manufacturers have learned some painful lessons that, in retrospect, should have been obvious. The idea that a design engineer knows exactly what users want, for example, has proved false, Flexibility in design and architecture has been the hallmark of successful PCs, although there are a few specialized markets where this does not apply. As one design engineer put it, “A PC is a tool, not an appliance.”
"Optical Computing: Fact, Fiction, and Fantasy" is the title of a talk BDM Corp.'s Athale likes to give.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: From Jennys to jets
abstract: Airplanes do not pervade our lives to the same extent as do other modern developments, as for example automobiles. Yet the impact planes have had on our modern culture, despite their short history, is enormous. For most of us the use of commercial airlines to routinely attend business meetings has become a fact of life, and the number of our neighbors and acquaintances who have flown for business or pleasure has increased dramatically in the last decade.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Our expansive past and explosive future
abstract: Preparing oneself to practice the profession of electrical engineering is somewhat like trying to take a drink from a firehose. The torrent (read “information”) comes too fast and under high pressure. And after the student is finished drinking, the gusher continues.

articleTitle: Profitability and safety: Deregulation encourages airlines to reduce operating costs to stay competitive, while imperiling traditional safety practices
abstract: The U.S. airline industry is in turmoil. Deregulation - the abandonment in 1978 of a system under which the now-defunct Civil Aeronautics Board maintained tight control over airlines, telling them what routes to fly and what fares they could charge - has brought airline competition on a scale never before seen in the United States. And with it have come new problems for airline managements, maintenance technicians, and flight personnel.

articleTitle: Personal computers: Fewer developments hut nevertheless important ones mark a year characterized by less-than-expected growth
abstract: In most industries, growth of 23 percent in one year would not be considered cause for alarm. But in the rollicking personal-computer industry, where growth of more than 50 percent a year for the foreseeable future once seemed like a sure thing, last year's 23 percent expansion has the experts wondering what went wrong.

The intention of General Electric to acquire the RCA Corp. came as a blockbuster. Yet Monday-morning quarterbacks insisted the takeover was not improbable. GE's aggressive chairman, John F. Welch Jr., had put the corporate giant in a good position to execute such a coup. Among other things, he had divested over $5 billion worth of the corporation's businesses and reduced the workforce by nearly 100000.

Thirteen experts were invited to provide overviews of fundamental areas of electrotechnology for this annual state-of-the-art review. Other inputs for the issue were obtained from some 80 contributors, many of whom are leaders within the IEEE's technical Societies. Introduced this year is a new section, “The specialties.” It covers fields more specialized than those discussed elsewhere in the issue: data encryption, communication codes, knowledge support systems design, engineering education, computer-aided design, and electromagnetic compatibility.
From time to time I have decried the absence of engineers on contemporary lists of heroes. We find plenty of pop singers and politicians, a few religious leaders, and an occasional sports hero.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Verification and arms control
abstract: It sometimes seems useful to compare the complexities of peacekeeping at an international level with those involving two neighbors.

Wouldn't it be appropriate if the major U.S. research universities would get together in a cooperative effort to influence the curriculum and the quality of instruction in public schools at the precollege level? It is widely known through the many reports published in recent years that the teaching of science, mathematics, and even English in elementary and secondary schools has deteriorated.

articleTitle: Protocols for communicating in the factory
abstract: Only 15 percent of the 40000 programmable tools, instruments, controls, and systems already installed at General Motors facilities are able to communicate with one another. When such communication does occur, it is costly, accounting for up to 50 percent of the total expense of automation because of the special wiring and the custom hardware and software interfaces needed.

articleTitle: The lure of molecular computing: While marketable products seem decades away, researchers are crystallizing theories and devices that will give biological organisms the power to compute
abstract: A splinter suddenly punctures your finger and lodges beneath the skin. Harmful bacteria begin to enter your bloodstream. A white blood cell recognizes a molecular structure on the surface of one of the invaders as it brushes by, triggering an elaborate sequence of defensive actions. This sequence, a cascade of chemical reactions within and between cells, occurs without any electric signals from nerves. In time, your finger swells, a dramatic macroscopic readout of these chemical and cellular events.

articleTitle: Optical-fiber sensors challenge the competition: Resistance to corrosion and immunity to interference head the list of benefits in detecting stimuli ranging from pressure to magnetism
abstract: After eight years of development, optical-fiber sensors are no longer brash upstarts, newcomers in the neighborhood. Through alteration of light by external stimuli, these sensors can now detect virtually any stimulus that other sensors can - from pressure and magnetism to acidity and acceleration - and often more sensitively and accurately, over a wider dynamic range.

articleTitle: Discrete-event simulation: When prototyping of large, complex systems is impossible, this technique, based on known behaviors of interacting elements, is useful
abstract: A group of scientists and engineers at AT&T Bell Laboratories, working on a communications network, was faced with a problem: develop a design that was resistant to damage and overload. Building a prototype would have taken years. The engineers took a dual approach to the problem that cut development time to a manageable level while still assuring the reliability of the design.

articleTitle: Optical detectors: Three contenders: Depending on the application, the photoeonductor, p-i-n diode, or avalanche photodiode may prove the best choice
abstract: The photodetector, a critical component of any fiber-optic communication system, has sometimes been overlooked in the recent tendency to concentrate on improving laser transmitters and the fibers themselves. Yet simply changing from one type of photo-detector to another can increase the capacity of an existing fiber-optic system by an order of magnitude - without touching any other component. For that reason, among others, many research laboratories are developing new photodetectors that might be installed in operating systems in the field in just a few years.

articleTitle: Coming from Detroit: Networks on wheels: Multiplexed wiring in new models promises cost-effective control and accurate diagnostics, as well as fewer wires and less redundancy
abstract: The ever-increasing electronic content of cars is a mixed blessing for carmakers. Advanced electronic features like antilock braking, electronic steering, and electronically controlled transmissions and suspensions can improve performance and promote the sale of cars. But the wiring, components, and electronic control units required for these systems must fight for space in today's smaller cars, where they may invite diagnostic and repair problems.

articleTitle: Helping computers communicate: The Open Systems Interconnection model promises compatibility for a variety of computer systems, although not all its functions are yet defined
abstract: Computers made by different companies ordinarily do not “talk” to one another. This aloofness sometimes applies even to different types of computers made by the same company. And when it comes to computerized systems, like machine tools and automatic teller machines, the communications problems can be nightmarish. Aside from expensive customized adapters and software links, compatibility remains an elusive target of the computer industry.

articleTitle: Coding speech at low bit rates: Advanced algorithms and hardware for voice telecommunications are paring hit rates by at least a factor of four, without losing intelligibility
abstract: New digital coding techniques arc emerging that promise to dramatically enhance the applicability of voice communications and storage. The techniques allow more speech to be represented with a given number of binary digits, without losing natural voice quality.

articleTitle: Zero-defect software: The elusive goal: It is theoretically possible but difficult to achieve; logic and interface errors are most common, but errors in user intent may also occur
abstract: In October 1960, shortly after a new radar network to warn the United States of missile attacks had become operational, a radar station in Greenland reported the appearance of a massive attack - a large number of radar returns coming over the eastern horizon. The real cause of the alarm: the moon was rising.

articleTitle: All-digital jets are taking off: Aboard developmental commercial and military aircraft, digital electronics score high in compactness, control flexibility, and reliability
abstract: Aircraft are undergoing a digital metamorphosis. Both civilian and military jets are emerging with second-generation digital avionics that promise more compact, more reliable, and highly flexible electronic systems.

articleTitle: Can power engineering education be re-energized?
abstract: In the typical college engineering department in the United States, students flock to electronics engineering courses in numbers large enough to make professors worry about overextending their resources. But down the hall in the same department, their colleagues who teach the power engineering courses are more likely to be worried for the opposite reason: they are having trouble attracting enough students or faculty members to keep their program going.

articleTitle: JIT is made to order: Beginning with the obvious goal of cutting costs by reducing inventories, just-in-time production now embraces an assortment of sound industrial practices
abstract: At Hewlett-Packard Co.'s plant in Cupertino, Calif., home of the HP 3000 Series 68 minicomputer, the time it takes to assemble a set of 31 printed-circuit boards has been slashed from 15 days in 1982 to 11.3 hours in 1986. During the same period, the inventory of circuit board work in process was cut from $670 000 to $20 000, and the number of back orders was reduced from an average of 200 to two.

articleTitle: Eyes for automatons: Faster, more accurate, and more consistent than humans can hope to be, machine vision systems are on their way to broad application
abstract: A growing number of industries are demanding machines that not only work flawlessly at high speed but can also see what they are doing. Image data is growing in importance as part of the great amount of information that computers need for controlling industrial processes, robots, and automated factories.

So begins the warning to users of a typical software package for personal computers. The programs are contained on subtly altered diskettes that prevent easy copying. After all, publishers of protected software reason, if copying a software package is as simple as putting the program disk in one drive and a blank disk in the other, what is to stop the user from making extras for friends or even for sale?

articleTitle: A review of progress at MCC: Although its current objectives do not include 'beating Japan,' this U.S. organization is positioned to help industry do so
abstract: The drums of publicity reverberated loudly when the Microelectronics & Computer Technology Corp. was formed - but not for long. After being set up in 1983 by 10 otherwise competing U.S. computer and semiconductor companies to upstage Japanese computer advances, MCC remained silent about its work. After declaring its goal - making the founding shareholders able to introduce 'fifth-generation' computer technology before Japan did - it faded from public view.

articleTitle: Electric utilities: Poised for deregulation?: Competitive forces are an outgrowth of technical advances, regulatory constraints, and a slackening in the growth of demand
abstract: The Houston Lighting & Power Ca in Texas says it has more electricity than it can sell, but a Federal law requires it to buy still more.

articleTitle: Counting the weapons: Many top secret eyes in the skies keep vigil over Soviet weponry: Just how sharp are they?
abstract: When a Titan 34D rocket exploded shortly after launching from Vandenberg Air Force Base in southern California in April, the accident sent chills through the U.S. intelligence community. The classified cargo of the rocket was a reconnaissance satellite; it was the second such failure within nine months. Coming on the heels of the U.S. space shuttle Challenger disaster in January, it meant new surveillance satellites would be grounded for months. Worse yet, only one imaging satellite for intelligence was left in orbit.

articleTitle: A matter of margins: Aging radios, radars, and computers in a 23 000-element system help controllers route aircraft during their 45 million hours per year in U.S. airspace
abstract: Whenever you fly - on a commercial airplane, a corporate jet, or even your uncle's two-seater prop plane - if the pilot has filed a flight plan with a Federal Aviation Administration division, you become a part of the air traffic control system. If you fly under instrument flight rules, your plane is a blip on a radar screen somewhere. Its takeoff and landing are two operations among some 43 million that the U.S. air traffic control (ATC) system handles each year. Aircraft under ATC guidance spend 45 million hours annually in U.S. airspace.

articleTitle: A framework for computer design: Instead of starting off with a microprocessor, equipment designers must now select from among the many available bus standards before choosing hardware and software
abstract: All too often, engineers end up addressing the wrong issues when designing systems. In the selection of a bus, undue emphasis may be placed on largely irrelevant factors.

articleTitle: Making your PC behave like another
abstract: At work, a circuit designer analyzes digital circuit test data using a laboratory program written to run only on IBM PCs and compatible personal computers. But at home, the engineer uses the same program on a quite incompatible PC - his daughter's Commodore Amiga. He simply slides the diskette into a special drive attached to the Amiga and loads another program - a software PC emulator - into the Amiga.

articleTitle: Dubrovnik impasse puts high-definition TV on hold: A report on the turmoil in setting program standards concludes with a scenario for future developments
abstract: Not since the color television wars of the early 1960s, when the NTSC, PAL, and Secam standards established their territorial imperatives, has there been such heated controversy as over yet another color television system proposed as a global standard: HDTV, or high-definition television.

articleTitle: Monitoring the tests: Missile flights and test explosions are watched closely to determine whether an adversary's new weapons might upset the strategic balance
abstract: To the naked eye, the tail end of a Soviet missile test high above the Kamchatka Peninsula in northeastern Siberia is almost imperceptible. A cluster of tiny dots of light - the burning nose cones of 10 reentry vehicles - flare briefly as they arch earthward. To the hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of US, Defense Department sensors and computers in the region, the same fleeting event is a gold mine of data on the Soviet missile.

articleTitle: Helping engineers help themselves: Although largely an individual responsibility, professional development affects a company's ability to retain top-notch professionals
abstract: In the computer department of a public utility in the western United States, programmers were hired to work on three projects involving systems design and development. Although each project required specialized training, many of the programmers' skills were transferable across projects. When several of the employees expressed an interest in transferring to other projects to broaden their experience, the supervisors refused. The result? Morale dropped, and turnover among the programmers increased dramatically as they left to go elsewhere and expand their careers.

articleTitle: Recipe for reliability: Shake and bake: Environmental stress screening (ESS), a military convention, is moving into other markets as an inexpensive way to improve product reliability and identify design flaws
abstract: In most functional testing of electronic systems, engineers hope that as many units as possible will pass the test. But environmental stress screening, or ESS, takes a different tack: its goal is to make as many units as possible fail.

articleTitle: The compact disk ROM: Applications software: It optimizes access time, is compatible with various operating systems, and has the potential for multimedia use
abstract: Given the specialty of the compact-disk, read-only memory - putting massive databases on a user's desk inexpensively - many engineers will likely find themselves perfecting the technology and expanding its uses for years to come. A spinoff of compact-disk audio technology, the optically read CD-ROM presents various challenges to computer software and systems engineers:

articleTitle: Amorphous silicon: from promise to practice
abstract: Twenty years ago, amorphous semiconducting devices were a radical concept. Today, they occupy a secure beachhead in the marketplace. Although the technology is still at a fairly early stage of development, recent commercial devices and others on the way assure the future of amorphous semiconductors.

articleTitle: Roboticists aim to ape nature: Engineers are thinking in new ways about sensing, chips, and robots as they study dolphins, slugs, and Homo sapiens
abstract: Three years ago, in the offices of the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, Lynn Conway, then director of Darpa's strategic computing program, decided that researchers in artificial intelligence needed fresh paradigms. Darpa had already challenged researchers to design a machine that could roam on its own through a wide range of environments in pursuit of some goal: spying, or seeking and destroying an enemy. Conway thought that the machine, called the autonomous land vehicle, might work better if it mimicked not human perception, cognition, and actions but those of, say, a cat.

articleTitle: Aerospace and military: Sandia builds a tough compact computer, the autonomous land vehicle takes a spin, and the Sergeant York gun is axed
abstract: Many military observers criticize the U.S. Department of Defense for emphasizing glamorous high-technology weaponry. It costs too much and is of dubious operational soundness and reliability, they contend. Others, however, maintain that advanced weapons systems can in fact be made effective and reliable. Moreover, they point out, such systems are critically needed as “force multipliers” to offset the numerical superiority of enemy forces.

articleTitle: A venerable giant sharpens its claws: General Electric's drive to increase profits and market share means drastic restructuring in product lines, employment, and manpower utilization
abstract: The announcement by the General Electric Co. last December that it planned to purchase the RCA Corp. seemed to take customers, employers, and the business community by surprise. In reality, the proposed acquisition was just one more in a series of well-planned moves that have been taking place at the giant corporation over recent years.

At 4:00 a.m., the disk subsystem of a critical mainframe computer breaks down. Within a few minutes, the computer operator has reached the manufacturer's expert troubleshooter by phone at home. A short exchange yields the probable cause of the failure, and the operator begins to take corrective action. Scenes like this have been common for years, but they may become rare. With software techniques now being put into practice, no one need be awakened from a sound sleep for an expert consultation.

articleTitle: The menacing microburst: Wind shear, the single greatest cause of air crashes in the United States, may soon begin to yield to technological solutions
abstract: Off a runway at Stapleton Airport in Denver, Colo., one warm afternoon in late May 1984, 14 airplanes waited in line to take off. Near the end of the line were two United Airlines jets, Flights 663 and 161. The pilots of the two Boeing 727s scanned the sky above Runway 35 Left for signs of dangerous weather. The pilot of Flight 663 decided that “it looked like a typical Denver afternoon” and elected to take off. The pilot of Flight 161 said the sky looked “spooky” and decided to wait until conditions changed.

articleTitle: Burning coal more cleanly and efficiently: Faced with tougher antipollution laws and inflationary costs, electric utilities turn to advanced coal combustion technologies
abstract: In the context of tougher antipollution laws and inflationary costs for electric utilities, advanced coal combustion technologies are discussed. The new technologies promise better pollution control at lower cost than attempts to patch the old systems; they also solve the utility problem of how to add small increments of generating capacity in only a few years. The discussion emphasizes fluidized-bed combustion and coal gasification which consume hydrocarbons and remove gaseous pollutants (such as sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide) during the combustion process itself. Integrating emission control into the combustion or gasification process is less costly, less energy-intensive, and more efficient than removing pollutants from the flue gas. Proponents maintain that the new alternatives make better use of utility and ratepayer money.

articleTitle: Underground nuclear weapons testing: despite improvements in simulation techniques, weapons designers defend their need for 'live' testing to help maintain the us. nuclear deterrent
abstract: Beneath a stretch of mesas and bone-dry lake beds some 100 miles north of Las Vegas, Nev., at least 16 nuclear warheads were detonated last year, releasing enough energy to destroy a dozen major cities. Since 1951 the United States has exploded more than 680 bombs above and below this landscape, broken only by clumps of sagebrush, scraggy grass, and craters.

articleTitle: When reactors reach old age: Can an obsolete nuclear power plant site he safely and economically restored to its original environmental condition?
abstract: Pacific Gas & Electric Co. shut down its Humboldt Bay nuclear reactor in California in 1976; for seven years, the utility didn't know what to do with it. In 1983, finally, it decided that the best action was to delay action - it locked up the reactor building and put off dismantling and burying it until the year 2015.

articleTitle: Assessing Japan's role in telecommunications: Building on successes in devices and small systems, Japan's R&D turns to making the large systems in which the United States has excelled
abstract: Trade in telecommunication products between the United States and Japan, now out of balance by $1.8 billion, will probably tip even further in favor of Japan in the 1990s, according to a panel of US. experts in telecommunications working under the US. initiative known as the Japanese Technology Evaluation Program (JTECH).

articleTitle: The puzzle of Chernobyl: Taken by surprise, technologists pose scenarios, map the radiation plume, and call for better emergency notification
abstract: News of the event itself - the world's worst nuclear reactor accident - emerged in an agonizing trickle. Answers about the cause of the explosion at Chernobyl and what can be done to prevent similar catastrophes in the electric utility industry may be even slower in coming. But already top nuclear experts in the United States and Europe have put forth plausible hypotheses.

articleTitle: How NASA prepared to cope with disaster: Extensive plans were in place to mitigate the effects of a shuttle failure, whether on the launch pad or aloft
abstract: In early February, in the wake of the explosion of the space shuttle Challenger a minute and a half after liftoff on the morning of Jan. 28, President Ronald Reagan appointed a commission to investigate the causes of the disaster. He has given the commission four months to analyze photographs of the scene, telemetry, debris, safety procedures, historical information, and other data to try to determine what happened.

articleTitle: Keeping them flying: airlines sometimes ignore maintenance problems to honor flight schedules - rather than canceling flights to make aircraft worthy by government standards
abstract: Every night, in airport hangars across the United States, mechanics licensed by the Federal Aviation Administration inspect and maintain aircraft in time for flights the following morning. Their tasks range from visual inspections and minor cabin repairs to troubleshooting faulty engines or cockpit instruments written up by pilots and flight engineers.

articleTitle: Electroluminescence catches the public eye: Rugged, readable, and compact, electroluminescent technology is breaking the price barrier: Designers are now using it in middle-range products
abstract: Marines from the Second Radio Battalion slid swiftly down a dangling rope in May 1985 from a CH-46 “Huey” helicopter as part of an exercise, Solid Shield 85, at Camp LeJeune, N.C. As the Huey hovered, a pulley was rigged to allow the marines on the ground to lower the cargo. First out was Alice (Aluminum Lightweight Individual Carrying Equipment), a pack containing a communications radio, batteries, and a 10-kilogram GRiDSE-T personal computer with an electroluminescent glass display. As Alice started its descent, the helicopter unexpectedly rose, jerking the pulley rope from the hands of a surprised marine. The pack plummeted 12 meters and slammed into the sandy ground. One of the marines rushed to the computer and turned it on. The EL display glowed orange-yellow, and he began typing in commands. In the finest U.S. Marine Corps tradition, the computer worked perfectly [Fig. 1].

articleTitle: Back on line in 72 hours: To reconnect Mexico City's complex electric grid after last September's earthquake, engineers zeroed in on the most critical repairs, aided by remote operation of substations
abstract: For Jorge Gutierrez Vera, last Sept 19 began like most other Thursdays in early autumn. In the cool morning air, he was ready to play a game of tennis at a racquet club in northwest Mexico City before going to his office at the local power authority. Suddenly, with an extended roar like an explosion, the earth pitched and shook violently.

articleTitle: Art analysis probing beneath the image: Electrotechnology backs up museum conservators in analyzing, conserving, and restoring works of art and in unmasking forgeries
abstract: Next time you see the Mona Lisa, in your mind's eye put a string of beads around her neck. The beads were discovered in January hidden on the woman herself - or, more precisely, on a digitized reproduction of the enigmatic portrait.
Clearly, much work needs to be done in every area of optical computing: materials, devices, algorithms, and architectures. And opinion varies on what the driver for the technology should be.

articleTitle: PC design: Architecture: Trading off technical innovation against the dependability of established standards is a principal consideration for PC designers
abstract: Before the IBM Corp. unveiled the PCjr in 1983, computer industry observers predicted that the new machine would take the home market by storm, its older sibling, the IBM PC, had grown from nothing to more than half the business market in the preceding two years, and sales in the millions were predicted for the diminutive “Peanut.” But in 1985, when IBM halted production, perhaps 200 000 PCjrs had been sold. Since then, another several hundred thousand have been sold at fire-sale prices.

articleTitle: The politics of peace pacts: Technical, monitoring capabilities are but part of the solution to arms control: Attitudes of the superpowers are becoming more crucial
abstract: When considering the future of arms control, one must brush Utopian rhetoric aside and accept that nuclear weapons are here to stay, say veteran arms controllers. When Mikhail S. Gorbachev proposes to banish nuclear weapons from the world by the year 2000, when Ronald Reagan declares his intent to render nuclear weapons “impotent and obsolete” experts like Milo Nordyke shake their heads and smile.

articleTitle: The real world: Controllers and technicians warn of a system stretched to its limits, citing mounting delays, overcrowded radio bands, and a rising number of near-misses
abstract: The two airliners - a United Airlines DC-4 and a Trans World Airlines Constellation - left Los Angeles international Airport under air traffic control on June 30, 1956, heading east. They cleared the terminal area routinely, but collided over the Grand Canyon. There was no nationwide system of real-time air traffic control in those days.

articleTitle: PC applications: Engineering: Only recently endowed with the power to do engineering chores, personal computers am already saving designers time and money
abstract: The personal computer is taking on a surprising role as a key component in engineering and science laboratories, traditionally the realm of the most powerful state-of-the-art computers.

articleTitle: 'Gold-plated' design: Redundancy and extremely high safety factors allow aircraft to withstand forces far exceeding those encountered during routine flights
abstract: Unlike the Concorde, the Boeing 727 was not designed to travel at the speed of sound or faster. But in the air over Saginaw, Mich., in April 1979, that is exactly what one did. A Boeing 727, spiraling in an uncontrollable dive from 39 000 feet, reached a calculated Mach number of 0.96 - enough to put parts of the craft into transsonic territory, based on the varying airspeeds around the fuselage.

articleTitle: Quebec hydro: La Grande tour: Three powerhouses, 200 dikes, and a vast flooded area near James Bay, Que., produce more electricity than any other hydroelectric complex in North America
abstract: Radisson, Que. - When the hydroelectric plant was being bulk here in northern Canada and activity was at a peak, 8000 workers hustled from “camp” through -45°C winter air to 10-hour shifts on the project. Now, since the plant runs pretty much unmanned, a mere 250 locals sustain this village.

Optical processors operated by the US. Department of Defense can perform calculations that would defeat a collection of the fastest Crays. “Yet the optical processors are solving real-world problems,” said one engineer, “Crays can solve them, but not fast enough. The solution is needed on the fly, not over the weekend.”

articleTitle: Communicating from the edge of the solar system: Centimeter-band transmissions, three-dimensional data compression, and laser-based systems may launch unmanned missions to deep space
abstract: It is one of the most challenging communications tasks ever: the creation of a “relay tower” in space, some 450 million miles (700 million kilometers) from earth. The tower will receive data from a half dozen instruments in a probe about 130000 miles (210000 km) away, and then transmit the data to earth - all without interruptions in communications and without any real-time human control of the tower.

articleTitle: PC design: Manufacturing: Although relatively simple to assemble, PCs contain highly complex parts; manufacturing them is more akin to making consumer goods than computer products
abstract: Personal computers are manufactured today in more ways than almost any other product, from fully automated plants where hardly a person disturbs the humming robots that build several machines each minute, to back room shops where a technician armed with only a screwdriver may produce 10 or 20 computers a day. Between these two extremes are assembly lines that use any imaginable mix of automated and manual operations; at the least, most lines use automated equipment for filling circuit boards with integrated circuits and soldering them in place.

articleTitle: PC applications: Directions: In the offing is more intuitive, more useful software than today's versions, thanks to more powerful microprocessors
abstract: As personal computers attain ever greater power, intriguing advances in software are promised to keep pace. But the evolution in both operating systems and applications will take place mostly behind the screen, leaving much future software similar to that of today.

“Computers are now at a midlife crisis,” said Alan Huang of AT&T Bell Laboratories. “Beyond 1 picosecond you begin dealing with optical frequencies anyway. So either you ignore the fact that it's optical frequencies or you make use of that fact. I am a digital computer person; most of the computers I've designed are electronic. Now I'm trying to move computers into a different technology that I believe is superior, which is optics. I want to build the world's fastest computer.” (Just for scale, 1 ps corresponds to a frequency of 1012 hertz, or a wavelength of about 300 micrometers in the far infrared.)
